analysis.one_liner: Restores a worker-friendly burden of proof in workplace discrimination cases involving hiring and promotion practices.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 12 bipartisan Senate cosponsors, never received a committee vote or a floor vote in either chamber before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: A 1989 Supreme Court decision (Wards Cove) made it harder for workers to prove that a hiring test, requirement, or other neutral-sounding workplace rule discriminates in effect against a protected group. This bill would have written the older, stricter standard back into law: once a worker shows that a practice produces a racially or sexually skewed result, the employer would have to prove the practice is genuinely essential to doing the job. It also let workers challenge a whole hiring process at once instead of pinpointing one rule. The bill never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers — especially Black, Hispanic, and women workers — who are screened out by hiring tests, education requirements, or other practices that look neutral but exclude protected groups. Under the bill, they would no longer bear the burden of proving that each individual rule was discriminatory or unjustified; the employer would have to justify the practice as essential to the job.

how_it_helps.text: Once a worker demonstrates that an employment practice has a disparate impact by race, color, religion, sex, or national origin, the employer must show the practice is 'required by business necessity,' defined as essential to effective job performance [S2][S3].

A worker could challenge an entire hiring process as a group of practices, without having to identify which specific rule produced the skewed result; an employer is only excused from justifying a practice it proves does not contribute to the impact [S2][S3].

The bill was a response to the Supreme Court's June 1989 Wards Cove decision, which had shifted much of that burden back onto workers; the bill's title, 'Fair Employment Reinstatement Act,' reflects its aim of restoring the standard set in the 1971 Griggs v. Duke Power case (general policy context).

analysis.who_pays: Employers — businesses, unions, and employment agencies facing disparate-impact claims — would bear the cost of proving their screening practices are job-essential and of defending more lawsuits, and might have to drop tests or requirements they cannot justify.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers using tests and screening rules

drawbacks.text: Employers and their allies argued the bill would force them to abandon legitimate hiring tests and credentials they could not prove were 'essential,' raising the risk of hiring by numbers rather than qualifications — the objection that later sank a similar bill's first version (general policy context).

The burden shift would increase litigation exposure and legal costs for employers of all sizes, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge even while arguing it is the price of enforceable anti-discrimination law [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real: making employers prove their screening rules are job-essential gives workers a practical way to challenge discrimination by results rather than by intent, but it also exposes businesses to costly litigation and could push them to drop some useful qualification standards. The bill addressed the employer side somewhat by excusing practices shown not to contribute to an impact, but it asked employers to carry a substantially heavier legal burden than the Supreme Court had just allowed. Weighing the two, this is a genuine civil-rights strengthening measure with real compliance costs, not a one-sided giveaway.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee — the committee's only action after referring it was to ask the Labor Department for its opinion — and no committee or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum introduced the bill on June 23, 1989, three weeks after the Wards Cove decision, with 11 original cosponsors from both parties [S1][S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources, where it stayed for the rest of the 101st Congress [S5].
The committee's only further action was to request an executive comment from the Department of Labor on September 26, 1989; the bill was never reported out or voted on by either chamber [S5].

The underlying dispute was not resolved this way: Congress returned to the same burden-of-proof question in later years, and the resulting Civil Rights Act of 1991 became law only after a prior version passed but was vetoed (general policy context).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers came out ahead: without the bill, they kept the Supreme Court's post-Wards Cove burden of proof, under which workers must do more to show that neutral-seeming hiring practices are discriminatory. Workers who faced such practices gained nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers keeping the lighter legal burden

for.name: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum
for.role: U.S. Senator from Ohio; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Employment Reinstatement Act to shift the burden of proof in disparate-impact discrimination cases back to employers.

for.name: 2 of 45 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a small bipartisan base.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to itself, requested a Labor Department comment, and never held a markup or vote on it; the bill died there.

against.name: President George H.W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation restoring the pre-Wards Cove disparate-impact standard, calling it a quota bill, and later vetoed a similar civil rights bill in 1990.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was mostly Democratic (10 of 55 Senate Democrats) but included 2 of 45 Senate Republicans, so the bill had modest bipartisan backing even though no vote was ever held.

industries.industry: U.S. employers (especially those using hiring tests and screening criteria)
industries.note: The bill would have required employers to prove job-essentiality for any practice producing a skewed hiring result, exposing them to more lawsuits and forcing changes to tests, credentials, and requirements. Employer groups fought to keep the post-Wards Cove standard, which places that burden on the worker instead.

Vendors whose standardized tests and screening products feed employer hiring decisions would face customers needing to justify those products as business necessities, threatening sales where the tools produce racially or sexually skewed outcomes.
